A chattel is any item of personal property that you own — something that belongs to you and can be moved, bought, sold, or transferred. Think of it as "stuff you own that isn't land or a building."

Your car, your furniture, your jewelry, your livestock, your phone — all of these are chattels. The ground your house sits on is not a chattel. The house itself (permanently fixed to the ground) is generally not a chattel either. But the couch inside the house? Chattel.
Why This Word Even Exists (The Real vs. Personal Split)

In law, all property is split into two big buckets:

Real property — Land and anything permanently attached to it (buildings, in-ground structures). This is where words like "real estate" come from.

Personal property — Everything else you own. And "chattel" is essentially the formal legal word for personal property, particularly physical, movable things.

So whenever lawyers or legal documents say "chattel," mentally translate it to: a piece of personal property, especially something physical and movable.
The Two Official Types of Chattels

Legal language divides chattels into two categories. You don't need to memorize these labels, but knowing them fills in the full picture:

1. Chattels Personal
These are your straightforward, everyday owned things — items you can physically pick up and take with you. A bicycle, a painting, a bag of rice, a herd of cows. These are the "purest" form of chattels. Within this category, lawyers sometimes split things further:

  • Choses in possession — physical things you can actually hold and touch (a watch, a laptop).
  • Choses in action — non-physical rights that still count as your property, like a debt someone owes you, a copyright, or shares in a company. You can't hold them in your hand, but you own them and can enforce them legally.

2. Chattels Real
This is the tricky one — don't let the name confuse you. Despite having the word "real" in it, a chattel real is not real estate. It refers to a temporary or limited interest in land, the most common example being a lease. When you rent an apartment, you hold a leasehold interest — a right to occupy land/property for a fixed period of time. That interest is yours, it has value, you can even transfer it — but since you don't permanently own the land, the law classifies it as personal property (a chattel), not real property. Hence: chattel real — it's related to real estate, but it's still classified on the personal property side.
The Most Important Historical Use: Chattel Slavery

This is where the word carries its heaviest moral and historical weight, and no complete explanation of "chattel" is honest without covering it.

In chattel slavery, enslaved human beings were legally classified as chattels — as property owned by another person. Just like a cow or a piece of furniture, they could be bought, sold, inherited, gifted, used as loan collateral, and passed down through a slaveowner's will. They had no legal personhood of their own.

The phrase "chattel slavery" is used by historians to specifically describe this form of slavery — where ownership of a person was total, permanent, and heritable — to distinguish it from other historical forms of forced labor (like debt bondage or indentured servitude, where the arrangement was at least theoretically limited or temporary). Chattel slavery was the dominant system in the American South, the Caribbean, and much of colonial South America. The word "chattel" in this context is not a euphemism — it was the actual legal term used in property law to categorize enslaved people.

While "chattel" is a somewhat old-fashioned word that rarely comes up in everyday conversation, it remains very much alive in legal and financial writing. A few common phrases:

  • Chattel mortgage — A loan arrangement where a movable asset (like a vehicle or piece of equipment) is put up as collateral. If you don't repay the loan, the lender can take the item.
  • Chattel paper — A legal document recording both a debt and a security interest in specific goods.
  • Personal chattel / goods and chattels — An old-fashioned but still occasionally used phrase meaning all of someone's movable personal belongings. ("All his goods and chattels were auctioned off.")

If you want a single mental anchor for this word:

Chattel = anything you personally own that isn't land or permanently fixed to land.

It's your stuff. It's movable. It's transferable. It belongs to you as an individual, not tied to the earth. At its darkest, the word has been applied to human beings who were stripped of their personhood and owned as property — which is why the word still carries a serious, weighty tone whenever it appears.
